usage: Very common about feelings and health
examples: 날씨가 좋아졌어요
The weather got better
Simple weather change, past tense
요즘 컨디션이 좋아지고 있어요
My condition is getting better these days
-고 있어요 shows the change is ongoing
약을 먹으니까 몸이 많이 좋아졌어요
After taking medicine my body got a lot better
-으니까 gives the cause of the improvement
nuance: 좋아지다 is the adjective 좋다 (good) plus -아지다, the pattern that turns a state-word into 'become that state', so it literally means 'come to be good' — a gradual drift from worse to better, not a fixed quality. The key contrast is 좋다 vs 좋아지다: 좋다 just says something IS good right now (기분이 좋아요 = I feel good), while 좋아지다 reports a CHANGE toward good (기분이 좋아졌어요 = I feel better than before). It is warm and neutral in register, fine in both 반말 and 존댓말, and shows up constantly with 몸(body), 기분(mood), 날씨(weather), 사이(relationship), and 실력(skill). The classic English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 좋다 when you really mean a transition — 'My Korean got better' is 좋아졌어요, never 좋았어요, because 좋았어요 just means 'it was good (in the past)'. Note too that 좋아지다 means 'come to like' when the subject is a person feeling (그 사람이 좋아졌어요 = I came to like that person), so context decides between 'get better' and 'grow fond of'.

mistakes: Saying 기분이 좋았어요 to mean 'my mood improved' — 좋았어요 only means 'I felt good (back then)' with no sense of change; for the improvement you need 좋아졌어요.
Treating 좋아지다 like a normal adjective and trying 좋아지다예요 — it is a verb (좋다 + 아지다), so the present is 좋아져요, never *좋아지다예요.

Using 좋아지다 for someone improving a thing on purpose; 좋아지다 is intransitive (it happens by itself). To say 'I improved my grades' you act on them with a different verb — 좋아지다 only describes the grades themselves getting better.

usage: Said to friends not seen in years
Often about losing love or interest
examples: 하늘 색이 변했어요
The color of the sky changed
Simple visible change, past tense
요즘 그 친구가 좀 변한 것 같아요
That friend seems to have changed a bit lately
-ㄴ 것 같아요 softens it to an impression
사람 마음은 언제든지 변할 수 있어요
A person's heart can change at any time
변할 수 있어요 expresses possibility
nuance: 변하다 is Sino-Korean: 變 (byeon, 'change, transform') + 하다, so it carries the feeling of something turning into a different state on its own, by nature or over time. The sharp contrast English speakers must learn is 변하다 vs 바꾸다: 변하다 is intransitive — the thing changes by itself (날씨가 변해요 = the weather changes), while 바꾸다 is transitive — somebody deliberately swaps or replaces a thing (계획을 바꿔요 = I change the plan). A related pair is 변하다 vs 바뀌다 (the passive of 바꾸다): 바뀌다 implies an external switch (신호등이 바뀌었어요 = the traffic light switched), whereas 변하다 implies inner transformation (성격이 변했어요 = his personality changed). Register is neutral and everyday. The big pitfall is using 변하다 with a direct object — you cannot say *계획을 변해요 to mean 'I change the plan'; if there is an actor doing the changing, you need 바꾸다. 변하다 only ever describes the subject itself becoming different.

mistakes: Saying 머리 스타일을 변했어요 for 'I changed my hairstyle' — 변하다 takes no object. Because you actively did it, use 바꿨어요 (from 바꾸다): 머리 스타일을 바꿨어요.

Confusing 변하다 with 바뀌다. If something was switched/replaced by an outside force (a schedule, a signal), Koreans say 바뀌었어요; reserve 변했어요 for internal transformation like feelings, color, or personality.
Over-using 변하다 for small everyday swaps. 'I changed my clothes' is 옷을 갈아입었어요, not 옷이 변했어요 — 변하다 would weirdly mean the clothes themselves morphed.

examples: 한국어 실력이 많이 늘었어요
My Korean skill improved a lot
The most natural way to say you got better at a language
요즘 운동을 안 해서 살이 늘었어요
I haven't exercised lately so I gained weight
-아서 links cause to the weight gain
연습하면 실력이 늘 거예요
If you practice, your skill will improve
Note 늘 거예요 — the ㄹ stays before 거예요
nuance: 늘다 means an amount, number, or ability grows bigger, and it is the everyday word for skills improving — 실력이 늘다 is THE phrase for 'getting better at something'. It is a ㄹ-irregular verb: the final ㄹ drops before endings beginning with ㄴ, ㅂ, or ㅅ, which is why the formal present is 늡니다 (not *늘습니다) — the ㄹ vanishes before -ㅂ니다. Watch the synonym split: 늘다 is intransitive (the thing increases by itself — 실력이 늘어요), while its causative twin 늘리다 is transitive (you increase a thing on purpose — 시간을 늘려요 = I extend the time). Compare also 증가하다, the stiff Sino-Korean 'increase' used in reports and statistics (인구가 증가했다); 늘다 is the warm spoken equivalent. The English-speaker pitfall is two-fold: first, forgetting the ㄹ-drop and saying *늘습니다; second, saying 'I improved my Korean' as if you act on it — Koreans say 한국어가 늘었어요 (Korean increased) with the skill as the subject, not as an object you operate on.

Saying 나는 한국어를 늘었어요 with 를 — 늘다 takes no object. The skill is the subject: 한국어가 / 한국어 실력이 늘었어요.

examples: 가게 손님이 많이 줄었어요
The shop's customers decreased a lot
Simple drop in numbers, past tense
요즘 일이 줄어서 좀 한가해요
Work has decreased lately so I'm a bit free
-어서 ties the decrease to having free time
용돈이 점점 줄고 있어요
My allowance is gradually shrinking
-고 있어요 plus 점점 stresses a slow ongoing fall
nuance: 줄다 is the exact opposite of 늘다 — it means an amount, number, or size gets smaller — and the two are learned as a pair (늘다/줄다). Like 늘다 it is a ㄹ-irregular verb, so the ㄹ drops before -ㅂ니다, giving the formal 줍니다 (not *줄습니다). The crucial synonym contrast is 줄다 vs 줄이다: 줄다 is intransitive — the thing shrinks by itself (소리가 줄었어요 = the sound got quieter on its own), while 줄이다 is the causative — you deliberately reduce something (소리를 줄였어요 = I turned the sound down). Its formal report-style synonym is 감소하다 (Sino-Korean 減少, 'reduce-decrease'), used for statistics; 줄다 is the natural conversational word. The English-speaker pitfall mirrors 늘다: don't say *줄습니다 (the ㄹ drops to make 줍니다), and don't put an object with 줄다. 'I reduced my spending' needs the transitive 줄이다 (지출을 줄였어요); 'my spending decreased' uses 줄다 with the subject particle (지출이 줄었어요).

Saying 살을 줄었어요 to mean 'I lost weight' — 줄다 takes no object, so it's 살이 줄었어요 (with 이). If you mean you deliberately slimmed, Koreans more often say 살을 뺐어요 (from 빼다).

usage: Comforting a sick or worried person
examples: 감기가 다 나아졌어요
My cold got completely better
Simple recovery, past tense
병원에 다녀온 후로 상태가 나아지고 있어요
Since going to the hospital my condition has been improving
-고 있어요 marks the recovery as in progress
힘들겠지만 시간이 지나면 나아질 거예요
It'll be hard, but things will improve with time
Standard words of comfort
nuance: 나아지다 is built from 낫다 ('to be better / to recover') plus -아지다 ('become'), so it specifically means coming UP from a bad or sick state — recovery and relief — which gives it a more emotional, hopeful color than the neutral 좋아지다. The contrast worth fixing: 좋아지다 simply moves from less-good to more-good (날씨가 좋아졌어요), while 나아지다 implies there was something WRONG that is now getting better — illness, a slump, a hard situation (몸이 나아졌어요, 형편이 나아졌어요). Because the root is 낫다 (a ㅅ-irregular: 낫다 → 나아), the spelling is 나아지다 with two ㅏ vowels and NO ㅅ. The classic English-speaker error is exactly that spelling: learners write *낫아지다, keeping the ㅅ, but the ㅅ of 낫다 drops between vowels, leaving 나아지다. Also note the bare root 낫다 alone already means 'get well' (감기가 나았어요 = my cold got better), so 낫다 and 나아지다 overlap for illness; 나아지다 just adds the gradual 'becoming' nuance and stretches to situations, not only bodies.

Saying 빨리 좋아지세요 to wish someone well — it's understood but not idiomatic. The set phrase for 'get well soon' is 빨리 나으세요 or 빨리 나아지세요, because recovery is exactly 나아지다's job.

usage: Very common way to calm someone
긴장 used as a noun with 풀리다
긴장되다 — the feeling comes over you
examples: 면접 때문에 너무 긴장했어요
I was so nervous because of the interview
Simple cause + nerves, past tense
발표 전에는 항상 조금 긴장해요
I always get a little nervous before a presentation
Habitual present with 항상
너무 긴장하지 말고 천천히 하세요
Don't be too nervous, just take it slow
Reassuring -지 말고 + advice
nuance: 긴장하다 is Sino-Korean: 緊 (gin, 'tight') + 張 (jang, 'stretch') + 하다, literally 'to be tightly stretched' — a vivid image of nerves pulled taut before a big moment. It describes performance-type nerves (tests, interviews, stages, sports), the keyed-up tension you feel when stakes are high. The key contrast is 긴장하다 vs 무섭다 vs 걱정하다: 무섭다 is 'to be scared/afraid' of a threat (귀신이 무서워요 = ghosts are scary); 걱정하다 is 'to worry' about an outcome over time (시험이 걱정돼요 = I'm worried about the exam); but 긴장하다 is the immediate bodily tension of a high-pressure moment — your heart pounds, your shoulders stiffen. Note the very common passive-feel form 긴장되다 ('to get nervous', the feeling arising in you) — 긴장돼요 often sounds more natural than 긴장해요 for 'I feel nervous right now'. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping every 'nervous' to one word: 'I'm nervous about the future' is really worry (걱정), not 긴장; reserve 긴장하다 for that taut, just-before-it-happens tension.

Forming the negative as 안 긴장해요 — with 하다 verbs built on a noun, the 안 splits inside: 긴장 안 해요 is the natural negative.

usage: You can relax / set your mind at ease
Polite reassurance to a customer or elder
안심 as a noun with 되다
examples: 무사하다는 소식을 듣고 안심했어요
I felt relieved to hear they were safe
Simple cause + relief, past tense
아이가 집에 잘 도착해서 이제 안심해요
The child arrived home safely so now I'm at ease
-아서 links the safe arrival to relief
제가 옆에 있으니까 안심하세요
I'm right here, so please rest assured
-으니까 reason + comforting command
nuance: 안심하다 is Sino-Korean: 安 (an, 'peace, safe') + 心 (sim, 'heart') + 하다, literally 'to make the heart peaceful' — that settling of the chest when a worry finally lifts. It is the natural pair-opposite of 걱정하다 (to worry): you 걱정하다 while the danger looms and 안심하다 once you know it's fine. The contrast you must keep clear is 안심하다 vs 안전하다, which look almost identical but differ by one syllable and one part of speech: 안심하다 is a VERB about a person's FEELING of relief (저는 안심했어요 = I felt relieved), while 안전하다 is an ADJECTIVE about a thing being SAFE (여기는 안전해요 = this place is safe). They share the 安 hanja, which is why beginners blur them. 안심하다 also commonly appears as 안심이 되다 ('to become reassured', feeling-driven) and in the warm imperative 안심하세요 ('rest assured'), which businesses and caretakers use a lot. The English-speaker pitfall is swapping in 안전하다 for the emotion — *저는 안전했어요 wrongly says 'I was safe', not 'I felt relieved'; relief is always 안심.

examples: 시험 결과에 실망했어요
I was disappointed in the test result
Note the particle: 에 marks what let you down
저는 웬만하면 실망 안 해요
I don't get disappointed easily
Negative with 실망 안 해요
기대가 컸던 만큼 실망도 컸어요
The bigger the hope, the bigger the letdown
Idiomatic 만큼 pairing hope and disappointment
nuance: 실망하다 is Sino-Korean: 失 (sil, 'lose') + 望 (mang, 'hope') + 하다, literally 'to lose hope' — the heart sinking when reality falls short of what you expected. That hanja root is the key to using it right: 실망 needs a prior expectation that wasn't met, so it's about LETDOWN, not plain sadness. The contrast English speakers must master is 실망하다 vs 슬프다: 슬프다 is 'to be sad' about a loss or sorrow with no expectation involved (강아지가 죽어서 슬퍼요 = I'm sad because my dog died), while 실망하다 specifically means a hope was dashed (성적에 실망했어요 = I'm disappointed by my grades). The defining grammar point is the particle: the thing that disappoints you takes 에 (결과에 실망했어요), and the PERSON who disappoints you takes 에게/한테 (그 사람에게 실망했어요 = I'm disappointed in that person). There's also a transitive partner 실망시키다 ('to disappoint someone', 부모님을 실망시켰어요 = I let my parents down). The English-speaker pitfall is calquing 'disappointed IN/WITH' as 와/하고 or no particle — Koreans mark the cause with 에 (for things) or 에게/한테 (for people), never with 'with'.

The contrast English speakers must master is 실망하다 vs 슬프다: 슬프다 is 'to be sad' about a loss or sorrow with no expectation involved (강아지가 죽어서 슬퍼요 = I'm sad because my dog died), while 실망하다 specifically means a hope was dashed (성적에 실망했어요 = I'm disappointed by my grades).

Marking the cause with the wrong particle. 'Disappointed in the result' is 결과에 실망했어요 (thing → 에); 'disappointed in him' is 그에게/그한테 실망했어요 (person → 에게/한테). English 'in/with' does not map to 와/하고.
Confusing 실망하다 (you feel let down) with 실망시키다 (you let someone else down). 'I disappointed my parents' is 부모님을 실망시켰어요, not 부모님을 실망했어요.

usage: After a kind act or touching moment
감동받다 — to receive deep emotion; extremely common
감동적 — adjective form for a moving thing
examples: 영화를 보고 감동했어요
I was moved by the movie
Simple cause + emotion, past tense
친구가 직접 케이크를 만들어 줘서 감동받았어요
My friend made me a cake by hand, so I was so touched
-아 줘서 (did for me) is what triggers the 감동
그 장면이 정말 감동적이었어요
That scene was really moving
Describing the thing with 감동적, not your own feeling
nuance: 감동하다 is Sino-Korean: 感 (gam, 'feel') + 動 (dong, 'move') + 하다, literally 'to be moved by feeling' — the heart stirred deeply by kindness, beauty, art, or a touching story. The contrast to lock in is 감동하다 vs 감사하다: 감사하다 means 'to be grateful / thank' for something done for you (도와주셔서 감사합니다 = thank you for helping), a social acknowledgment; 감동하다 is the inner emotional swell of being touched, which may bring tears, not a thank-you. They share the 感 ('feel') hanja, which is why learners conflate them. A crucial usage note: Koreans very often say 감동받다 (감동 + 받다, 'to receive deep emotion') and 감동하다 almost interchangeably for 'I was touched' — 감동받았어요 is arguably the more frequent spoken form. The cause is marked with 에 (그 말에 감동했어요 = I was moved by those words). To describe the thing itself as moving, use the adjective 감동적이다 (감동적인 영화 = a moving film), not 감동하다, which is reserved for the person feeling. The English-speaker pitfall is saying 감사하다 ('thank you') when you really mean you were emotionally moved — the two feelings are different, and Koreans keep them apart.

Marking the cause with the wrong particle or none. The trigger of emotion takes 에: 그 편지에 감동했어요 ('moved by that letter'), not 그 편지를 감동했어요.

usage: Praising someone after a long hardship
견디기 + 힘들다, a very common pattern
examples: 한여름 더위를 견뎠어요
I bore the midsummer heat
Simple object + endure, past tense
힘든 시간을 잘 견디고 있어요
I'm holding up well through the hard times
-고 있어요 shows the enduring is ongoing
조금만 더 견뎌 주세요
Please hold on just a little longer
Encouraging someone with -아 주세요
nuance: 견디다 means to withstand and hold out against something hard, painful, or long — hardship, heat, pain, loneliness, a tough stretch of life. It conjugates as a regular ㅣ-stem verb: 견디 + 어 contracts to 견뎌, giving 견뎌요 / 견뎠어요. The contrast that matters most is 견디다 vs 참다: 참다 is to hold back or suppress a single impulse or sensation in the moment — a laugh, a sneeze, anger, the urge to pee (웃음을 참았어요 = I held in my laughter), while 견디다 is to endure a prolonged ordeal over time (외로움을 견뎠어요 = I endured the loneliness). So 참다 = suppress a momentary urge; 견디다 = weather a lasting hardship. A near-synonym for the strong, gritty 'hold out' sense is 버티다 (버텨요), which adds a flavor of stubbornly hanging on against pressure; 견디다 is a touch more neutral and can include quietly bearing pain. The English-speaker pitfall is using 견디다 for a quick, one-off suppression — 'I couldn't bear to hold my pee' is 참다 (참을 수 없었어요), not 견디다, because that's a momentary urge; reach for 견디다 only when the suffering stretches over time.
